# Experiment Design: The Effect of QuaRot's Hadamard Transformation on Weight-Only Quantization Quality at 2–4 Bits

## 1. Objective and research questions

This document specifies a complete, self-contained experiment to answer two questions about weight-only low-precision quantization of large language models. The experiment has not been run; it is a design-only deliverable, and no result reported in this document is a measured outcome.

Part (a) asks *how* the Hadamard transformation used in QuaRot improves the quality of weight-only quantized models under low-precision settings. The working hypothesis, drawn from the QuaRot paper, is that outlier dimensions in LLM weights (a small number of entries whose magnitude is orders of magnitude above the mean) force per-group quantizers to waste most of the representable range on a handful of values, corrupting the long tail of small weights. Applying a random orthogonal Hadamard rotation W → WH before quantization spreads that outlier energy uniformly across dimensions, making the per-group weight distribution approximately Gaussian and therefore well matched to a symmetric affine codebook. Part (a) is therefore not merely "does QuaRot help" but "does the rotation reduce outlier-driven quantization error, and does that reduction propagate to downstream quality."

Part (b) asks whether QuaRot *stabilizes and improves* performance at 2–4 bit weight precision, i.e., in the regime where RTN and GPTQ degrade sharply or collapse. "Stabilize" is interpreted operationally (Section 5b): a method is judged to fail at a given (model, bit-width, metric) cell if degradation crosses a pre-registered threshold, and QuaRot is said to stabilize performance if its failure rate across cells is substantially lower than RTN's and GPTQ's at 2 and 3 bits, while its quality is at least as good as the best baseline at 4 bits.

Two design principles follow. First, the method effect must be separated from the algorithm effect: QuaRot (rotation + RTN) versus RTN confounds the rotation with the choice of error-minimizing vs. round-to-nearest algorithm, so the experiment includes a fourth arm, Hadamard-GPTQ, which differs from GPTQ by exactly the rotation. Second, the mechanism claim of part (a) requires weight-level diagnostics (outlier statistics, per-layer quantization error) in addition to task-level metrics, so that a causal chain — rotation reduces outliers → outliers reduce per-layer quantization error → error reduction reduces perplexity/task degradation — can be checked link by link.

## 2. Experimental design

### 2.1 Independent variables

The experiment is a factorial over two independent variables. The first is bit-width W ∈ {4, 3, 2}, applied identically to every arm. The second is the quantization method, with four arms described below. A third, within-arm variable is the Hadamard seed (Section 2.5), which varies only for the two rotation arms. Model is a blocking variable (Section 2.3), not a free factor: all arms and bit-widths are run on the same models so that every comparison is within-model.

### 2.2 The four arms and exact quantization configuration

All arms share one quantization configuration unless stated otherwise: per-group symmetric affine quantization with group size g = 128; the scale of each group is (max |w| − min |w|)/(2^W − 1) computed on the (possibly rotated) weights, offsets are not used (symmetric), and quantized codes are stored as W-bit integers. All linear layers of the model — attention projections (q, k, v, o), feed-forward up/down projections, and the language-model head (lm_head) — are quantized. Input token embeddings are kept in FP16. This layer selection matches the QuaRot paper's weight-only setting and the standard GPTQ configuration; it is flagged as assumption A10.

Arm 1, RTN: round-to-nearest quantization of the original weights with the shared configuration. No calibration data is used; the method is fully deterministic. This is the no-calibration baseline.

Arm 2, GPTQ: the Hessian-approximation, error-minimizing quantization of Frantar & Alistarh. Each linear layer is quantized by greedily choosing codes that minimize ‖WX − Q̂X‖² subject to a sparsity-ordered update, using the exact per-layer Hessian X X^T accumulated over the calibration set, with the standard Cholesky-factored inverse-Hessian schedule and oblique projection. GPTQ uses the same group size, symmetric per-group scaling, and layer set as RTN, so the only differences from Arm 1 are the use of the Hessian and the calibration data. GPTQ is deterministic given fixed calibration data and seed.

Arm 3, QuaRot (weight-only variant): each linear weight W is replaced by W' = W H, where H = (1/√d) S₁ H_d S₂ is a random orthogonal Hadamard matrix — S₁ and S₂ are independent random diagonal matrices with ±1 entries drawn from a fixed seed, and H_d is the size-d Walsh–Hadamard matrix (composed of tensor products of 2×2 Hadamard blocks, so it is applied in O(d log d) time). W' is quantized with the same per-group symmetric affine RTN configuration as Arm 1. At inference, the dequantized Ŵ' is multiplied by H on the activation side: Ŷ = X H Ŵ'^T, exploiting H = H^T and H^T H = I. The Hadamard application to activations is a runtime arithmetic operation, not activation quantization, so this arm respects the weight-only constraint. Note that the full QuaRot system also includes SmoothQuant activation smoothing; that component is an activation-side technique and is explicitly out of scope here, so this arm is the paper's weight-only component (Hadamard + RTN). This scoping is flagged as assumption A12 and as limitation L1.

Arm 4, Hadamard-GPTQ: the same rotation W' = W H is applied first, and GPTQ is then run on the rotated model — critically, the per-layer Hessian is recomputed on the rotated network (a forward pass of the rotated model over the calibration set), so the Hessian reflects the rotated weight/activation geometry rather than being carried over from the unrotated model. This arm differs from Arm 2 by exactly the rotation, and is the clean ablation that isolates the Hadamard step at fixed algorithm. It is the central comparison for part (a).

### 2.3 Model selection and justification

Three models are used: LLaMA-2-7B, LLaMA-2-13B, and Mistral-7B-v0.1. The justification is threefold. First, the QuaRot paper reports results on LLaMA-2, LLaMA-3, and Mistral, so using the same families makes the design's claims source-consistent and permits direct comparison with published numbers. Second, 7–13B models are the scale at which weight-outlier structure is pronounced and 2-bit quantization is visibly destructive; smaller models show the phenomenon less sharply. Third, including two different architectures (LLaMA and Mistral, with different attention variants and vocabularies) tests whether the conclusion is family-specific, which is necessary before claiming that QuaRot "stabilizes" 2–4 bit quantization generally rather than for one family. A 3B model would have been the minimal-budget alternative and a 70B model the maximal-strength alternative; both are rejected on budget grounds (Section 6) and noted as assumption A2.

### 2.4 Calibration data (GPTQ arms only)

RTN and QuaRot require no calibration. GPTQ and Hadamard-GPTQ use a fixed calibration set: 256 sequences of 2048 tokens sampled from the C4 validation split (en-10.0.0), using the standard GPTQ sampling procedure with a fixed sampling seed (42) and standard tokenization per model. The same calibration set is used for every model, every bit-width, and every seed of the two GPTQ arms, so calibration is a controlled variable, not a free one. Hadamard-GPTQ uses the identical sampling seed and sequences; only the forward pass (hence the Hessian) differs because the weights are rotated.

### 2.5 Seed strategy

The two rotation arms depend on the random sign matrices S₁, S₂. For each (model, W) cell, K = 5 independent Hadamard seeds are drawn from a documented list (e.g., 0–4), and each seed produces a fully independent quantized model and evaluation. This matters most at 2 bits, where rotation variance is largest and "stabilization" claims would otherwise amount to a single lucky draw; K = 5 supports variance estimates and paired tests. RTN and GPTQ are deterministic under fixed configuration and calibration, so they require a single run per cell. Total quantization runs: RTN 3 models × 3 W = 9; GPTQ 9; QuaRot 45; Hadamard-GPTQ 45; plus 3 FP16 reference evaluations.

## 3. Controls

Every variable that is not the target of a comparison is held constant across arms, and each control is listed with the reason it must be controlled. Group size g = 128 is identical across all four arms, because group size independently changes quantization granularity and would otherwise confound the method effect; a g ∈ {64, 256} sensitivity sweep is listed as assumption A7 but is not in the main design. Symmetric per-group affine scaling is used by all arms, because mixing symmetric and asymmetric codebooks would introduce a second algorithmic difference. The layer set (all linears including lm_head, embeddings FP16) is identical, because different layer coverage changes total effective bit-count and quality. The FP16/BF16 reference is the original, unmodified checkpoint for each model, evaluated with identical batching, sequence length, and prompt templates as the quantized models, so that every degradation number is a within-model difference. The calibration set is fixed in content, size, order, and sampling seed for both GPTQ arms, because GPTQ quality is sensitive to calibration data and an uncontrolled difference would corrupt the GPTQ-vs-Hadamard-GPTQ contrast. Evaluation protocol — dataset splits, prompt templates, batch size, seed for any stochastic decoding (all tasks here are greedy, so none), and hardware — is identical across arms, because benchmark harness differences are a known source of spurious perplexity deltas of the same order as the effects being measured. Hardware is a single node with the same GPU for all runs, because quantization kernels and precision of the dequantized matmul (FP16 accumulate of dequantized-to-FP16 weights) must be the same everywhere. Finally, the bit-width is applied identically to every arm, and dequantization at inference uses the same FP16 dequantized matmul in all arms, so the measured differences come from the quantization method alone, not from inference precision.

## 4. Evaluation protocol

### 4.1 Language-modeling perplexity

Zero-shot perplexity is computed on three held-out sets: WikiText-2 (test), C4 (validation, 256K-token window), and PTB (test), using the standard next-token evaluation with sequence length 2048 and batch 8, identical for FP16 and all quantized models. Perplexity is reported both as the absolute value and as relative degradation ΔPPL = (PPL_quant − PPL_FP16)/PPL_FP16. Three sets are used because the three corpora have different vocabulary coverage and domain, and a method that fails on one but not another is not "stabilized."

### 4.2 Zero-shot task suite

Six zero-shot tasks are evaluated with the lm-evaluation-harness, greedy decoding, default templates: LAMBADA (last-word prediction), PIQA (physical commonsense), ARC-e (science reasoning), WinoGrande (coreference), TruthfulQA (multiple-choice), and RTE (entailment). Accuracy is reported per task as FP16 value and Δaccuracy. The suite mixes generation-style and multiple-choice formats and spans commonsense, reasoning, and truthfulness, so that "quality" is not a single-number construct.

### 4.3 FP16 reference

For each model, the unmodified checkpoint is evaluated once on all three perplexity sets and all six tasks, with the exact protocol of 4.1 and 4.2. These nine numbers per model are the denominator of every degradation metric and the anchor of the failure rule; they are computed once and reused, never re-sampled.

### 4.4 Mechanism diagnostics (for part (a))

Three weight-level measurements are taken per layer, per model, and per arm: (i) outlier statistics — the ratio of maximum to mean absolute weight magnitude, the kurtosis of the weight distribution, and the effective number of bits (the entropy of the quantization codebook usage, i.e., how many of the 2^W codes are actually used, or equivalently 1 − normalized quantization MSE) — computed both on the original weights and, for the rotation arms, on the rotated weights W H; (ii) per-layer relative quantization error ‖Q(W) − W‖_F / ‖W‖_F (and, for rotation arms, ‖Q(WH)H^T − W‖_F / ‖W‖_F, which is the error the model actually sees); (iii) the Spearman correlation, across layers, between each layer's pre-rotation outlier ratio and its pre-rotation quantization error, and the same correlation computed post-rotation for the rotation arms. The predicted signature of the mechanism is: pre-rotation, high outlier ratio correlates strongly with high quantization error; post-rotation, outlier ratios are compressed across layers, the correlation weakens, and per-layer error drops in absolute terms. If QuaRot beats RTN but this signature is absent, the gain has a different cause and part (a) must be answered accordingly — the diagnostics are what make the "how" question answerable rather than merely correlational.

## 5. Analysis plan

### 5(a) Attributing quality gains to the Hadamard rotation

The rotation effect is estimated from two contrasts at each (model, W): C1 = RTN − QuaRot, which isolates rotation under RTN, and C2 = GPTQ − Hadamard-GPTQ, which isolates rotation under GPTQ. The causal chain is checked in three steps. Step 1 (rotation → outliers): compare pre/post-rotation outlier statistics; the expected result is a large drop in max/mean ratio and kurtosis in the rotated weights. Step 2 (outliers → error): compare the layer-level error-vs-outlier correlation pre- vs. post-rotation and the absolute per-layer relative quantization error of QuaRot vs. RTN and Hadamard-GPTQ vs. GPTQ; the expected result is a weaker correlation and lower error after rotation. Step 3 (error → quality): compare ΔPPL and Δaccuracy of the paired contrasts C1 and C2; the expected result is that the arms with lower weight-level error have lower quality degradation. If C1 and C2 both favor the rotated arm and steps 1–2 show the diagnostic signature, the gain is attributed to the rotation specifically; if only C1 (or only C2) favors rotation, the effect is algorithm-conditional; if the diagnostics show no outlier compression, the claim of part (a) is not supported and the design has failed in the informative direction.

### 5(b) Operational failure definition and sensitivity analysis

A method is declared to **fail** at a (model, W, metric) cell if any of the following holds: ΔPPL > 100% over the FP16 reference, or absolute PPL > 10, or Δaccuracy > 20 percentage points on any of the six tasks. The three clauses are pre-registered together with their rationale: the relative PPL clause captures multiplicative collapse (the typical 2-bit GPTQ/RTN failure mode), the absolute PPL clause captures cases where the FP16 baseline is already weak, and the accuracy clause captures task-level collapse that perplexity may miss. Part (b) is then answered by tabulating, for each method and each W ∈ {4, 3, 2}, the fraction of cells across the 3 models × 9 metrics in which the method fails, plus the worst-cell degradation. QuaRot "stabilizes" 2–3 bit quantization if its failure fraction at W = 2 and W = 3 is materially lower than both RTN's and GPTQ's, and "improves" if its mean degradation at those widths is lower than both baselines'. A sensitivity analysis repeats the failure tabulation at 50% and 150% of each threshold (i.e., ΔPPL > 50%/150%, PPL > 5/15, Δacc > 10/30 pts) to show that the conclusion is not an artifact of the exact cutoff. The pre-registration of the thresholds and the sensitivity sweep are the guard against post-hoc threshold shopping.

### 5(c) Statistical tests, effect sizes, and confidence intervals

All method comparisons are paired within (model, W, seed) cells: the two arms in a contrast are evaluated on identical data with identical protocol, so per-cell paired differences are the unit of analysis. For each contrast and metric, the paired difference (e.g., ΔPPL_GPTQ − ΔPPL_HadGPTQ at W, model, seed) is tested with the Wilcoxon signed-rank test (non-parametric because 2-bit degradation distributions are heavy-tailed and n per contrast is small: 5 seeds × 3 models = 15 pairs for rotation arms, 3 pairs for the deterministic-arm contrasts — the latter are reported descriptively with CIs rather than tested), with the rank-biserial correlation r as the effect size. 95% confidence intervals are computed by non-parametric bootstrap (10,000 resamples over the seed × model pairs) on the mean paired difference. Because the full analysis involves many cells (4 methods × 3 W × 3 models × 9 metrics), no multiplicity correction is applied to the primary table, but a Bonferroni-corrected version of the W = 2 and W = 3 comparisons is reported as a robustness check, and all cells — including null ones — are reported in the main table.

## 6. Feasibility

This is a **design-only deliverable; no experiment has been run**, and nothing in this document is a measured result. Feasibility is stated for a standard execution environment (not the current sandbox, which is CPU-only, network-disabled, and contains no code or data). Hardware budget: 1–2× NVIDIA A100-80GB (or equivalent) per model, single node; 80GB is required to hold a 13B model in FP16 plus GPTQ's Hessian workspace. Estimated wall time per run: RTN quantization of a 7–13B model at g = 128 takes on the order of 10–30 minutes; QuaRot adds the O(d log d) rotation, negligible; GPTQ takes on the order of 1–3 hours per (model, W) including the Hessian forward pass, and Hadamard-GPTQ is comparable plus the rotation. Evaluation of one quantized model on the three PPL sets plus six tasks takes on the order of 1–2 hours on a single A100. Per (model, W) cell the cost is therefore roughly: RTN ≈ 1.5–2 h, GPTQ ≈ 3–5 h, QuaRot ≈ 1.5–2 h (×5 seeds), Hadamard-GPTQ ≈ 3–5 h (×5 seeds), giving ≈ 30–40 GPU-hours per (model, W) cell, ≈ 90–120 per model, and ≈ 270–360 GPU-hours total for 3 models × 3 W × 4 arms (with seed multiplicity) plus 3 FP16 references. On 1× A100 this is roughly 12–15 days; on 2× A100 (models parallelized) roughly 6–8 days; a realistic single-team budget is **1–2× A100-80GB for 3–7 calendar days**, dominated by the 90 seeded rotation-arm runs. A reduced-budget variant (drop Mistral, K = 3 seeds) cuts this by roughly half. Software: the official QuaRot repository (Hadamard construction, rotation, and weight-only quantization), GPTQModel (or the original GPTQ-for-LLaMa code) for the GPTQ arms, Hugging Face Transformers for model loading and the FP16 reference, and lm-evaluation-harness for the task suite. One-time network access is needed at setup to fetch model weights and code; no network is needed during the runs. Storage: ≈ 3 models × ~25 GB FP16 ≈ 75 GB, plus quantized checkpoints (2–4 bits) totaling under 50 GB.

## 7. Assumptions and limitations

The following assumptions were flagged at the planning stage and are carried forward with their alternatives; they are choices, not fixed constraints. A1: Model family LLaMA-2 7B/13B + Mistral-7B — matters because the outlier phenomenon and the paper's comparability both depend on family; alternative: GPT-2 (weak outliers) or a single 3B model (cheapest). A2: Size band 7–13B — 2-bit effects are most visible at ≥7B; alternatives: 3B-only (minimal budget) or 70B (strongest claim, ~10× budget). A3: Calibration data C4 validation, 256 × 2048 tokens, seed 42 — affects only the two GPTQ arms but must be identical across them; alternative: WikiText-2 train split. A4: Benchmarks = 3 PPL sets + 6 zero-shot tasks — alternatives: PPL-only (cheaper, under-characterizes quality) or the full ~10-task suite (more expensive). A5: Failure rule ΔPPL > 100% / PPL > 10 / Δacc > 20 pts, pre-registered with sensitivity at 50%/150% — the entire part-(b) conclusion hinges on it; alternative: relative-only threshold or qualitative judgment. A6: Hadamard-GPTQ included as the fourth arm — without it, rotation and algorithm effects are confounded; alternative: drop it (weaker causal attribution). A7: Group size g = 128, symmetric per-group affine — matches standard QuaRot/GPTQ configuration; alternative: g ∈ {64, 256} sensitivity sweep (≈2× runs). A8: K = 5 Hadamard seeds per rotation-arm cell — needed to support "stabilize" claims at 2-bit; alternative: K = 1 (cheapest, but cannot distinguish stabilization from luck). A9: Wilcoxon signed-rank + rank-biserial r + bootstrap CIs, no primary multiplicity correction, Bonferroni as robustness check — alternative: plain mean±std reporting. A10: All linear layers including lm_head quantized, input embeddings FP16 — paper-consistent; alternative: keep lm_head FP16 (would flatter all arms equally). A11: Feasibility budget 1–2× A100-80GB, 3–7 days — the feasibility claim must name a concrete budget; alternative: single 40GB card, 7B-only. A12: Scope excludes SmoothQuant activation smoothing, activation quantization, and residual quantization — these are activation-side or out-of-scope components; alternative: include a runtime-overhead micro-benchmark as a secondary metric.

New limitations arising in the full write-up. L1: The "QuaRot" arm is the paper's weight-only component (Hadamard + per-group RTN), not the full QuaRot system with SmoothQuant; results therefore answer the question as scoped (weight-only), but any comparison with the paper's full-system numbers must keep this scoping in mind. L2: The Hadamard-GPTQ arm requires recomputing the Hessian on the rotated model; if an implementation carries the unrotated Hessian over, the arm is not the intended ablation — this must be verified in the implementation before runs. L3: The deterministic arms (RTN, GPTQ) have only 3 pairs per contrast (one per model), so their contrasts are reported descriptively with CIs rather than hypothesis-tested; the statistical power for part (a) rests on the 15-pair rotation contrasts. L4: The failure rule's accuracy clause (Δacc > 20 pts) is coarse for tasks whose FP16 accuracy is already high (e.g., PIQA), where a 20-point drop is near-impossible; the PPL clauses carry most of the part-(b) signal, and this asymmetry should be noted when interpreting the failure table. L5: Perplexity and task degradation are evaluated on a single prompt set per task (harness defaults); harness template or prompt-sampling differences across versions could shift absolute numbers, so the harness version must be pinned. L6: All conclusions are specific to the three models and three widths tested; generalization to other architectures, sizes, or W = 1 requires further runs. L7: The design assumes the named open-source implementations correctly implement the described configurations; a pre-flight sanity check (reproduce a published RTN/GPTQ 4-bit perplexity number within tolerance on LLaMA-2-7B) is recommended before the full grid is launched.

A reader with access to the named implementations (QuaRot repository, GPTQModel, Transformers, lm-evaluation-harness), the three model checkpoints, and 1–2× A100-80GB can execute this experiment from this document alone: quantize each model under each arm and bit-width with the seeds and calibration set specified, evaluate on the specified protocol, compute the specified diagnostics, and apply the specified analysis. No experiment has been run in producing this document.

## 1. Objective and research questions

This document specifies a complete, self-contained experiment to answer two questions about weight-only low-precision quantization of large language models. The experiment has not been run; it is a design-only deliverable, and no result reported in this document is a measured outcome.

Part (a) asks *how* the Hadamard transformation used in QuaRot improves the quality of weight-only quantized models under low-precision settings. The working hypothesis, drawn from the QuaRot paper, is that outlier dimensions in LLM weights (a small number of entries whose magnitude is orders of magnitude above the mean) force per-group quantizers to waste most of the representable range on a handful of values, corrupting the long tail of small weights. Applying a random orthogonal Hadamard rotation W → WH before quantization spreads that outlier energy uniformly across dimensions, making the per-group weight distribution approximately Gaussian and therefore well matched to a symmetric affine codebook. Part (a) is therefore not merely "does QuaRot help" but "does the rotation reduce outlier-driven quantization error, and does that reduction propagate to downstream quality."

Part (b) asks whether QuaRot *stabilizes and improves* performance at 2–4 bit weight precision, i.e., in the regime where RTN and GPTQ degrade sharply or collapse. "Stabilize" is interpreted operationally (Section 5b): a method is judged to fail at a given (model, bit-width, metric) cell if degradation crosses a pre-registered threshold, and QuaRot is said to stabilize performance if its failure rate across cells is substantially lower than RTN's and GPTQ's at 2 and 3 bits, while its quality is at least as good as the best baseline at 4 bits.

Two design principles follow. First, the method effect must be separated from the algorithm effect: QuaRot (rotation + RTN) versus RTN confounds the rotation with the choice of error-minimizing vs. round-to-nearest algorithm, so the experiment includes a fourth arm, Hadamard-GPTQ, which differs from GPTQ by exactly the rotation. Second, the mechanism claim of part (a) requires weight-level diagnostics (outlier statistics, per-layer quantization error) in addition to task-level metrics, so that a causal chain — rotation reduces outliers → outliers reduce per-layer quantization error → error reduction reduces perplexity/task degradation — can be checked link by link.

## 2. Experimental design

### 2.1 Independent variables

The experiment is a factorial over two independent variables. The first is bit-width W ∈ {4, 3, 2}, applied identically to every arm. The second is the quantization method, with four arms described below. A third, within-arm variable is the Hadamard seed (Section 2.5), which varies only for the two rotation arms. Model is a blocking variable (Section 2.3), not a free factor: all arms and bit-widths are run on the same models so that every comparison is within-model.

### 2.2 The four arms and exact quantization configuration

All arms share one quantization configuration unless stated otherwise: per-group symmetric affine quantization with group size g = 128; the scale of each group is (max |w| − min |w|)/(2^W − 1) computed on the (possibly rotated) weights, offsets are not used (symmetric), and quantized codes are stored as W-bit integers. All linear layers of the model — attention projections (q, k, v, o), feed-forward up/down projections, and the language-model head (lm_head) — are quantized. Input token embeddings are kept in FP16. This layer selection matches the QuaRot paper's weight-only setting and the standard GPTQ configuration; it is flagged as assumption A10.

Arm 1, RTN: round-to-nearest quantization of the original weights with the shared configuration. No calibration data is used; the method is fully deterministic. This is the no-calibration baseline.

Arm 2, GPTQ: the Hessian-approximation, error-minimizing quantization of Frantar & Alistarh. Each linear layer is quantized by greedily choosing codes that minimize ‖WX − Q̂X‖² subject to a sparsity-ordered update, using the exact per-layer Hessian X X^T accumulated over the calibration set, with the standard Cholesky-factored inverse-Hessian schedule and oblique projection. GPTQ uses the same group size, symmetric per-group scaling, and layer set as RTN, so the only differences from Arm 1 are the use of the Hessian and the calibration data. GPTQ is deterministic given fixed calibration data and seed.

Arm 3, QuaRot (weight-only variant): each linear weight W is replaced by W' = W H, where H = (1/√d) S₁ H_d S₂ is a random orthogonal Hadamard matrix — S₁ and S₂ are independent random diagonal matrices with ±1 entries drawn from a fixed seed, and H_d is the size-d Walsh–Hadamard matrix (composed of tensor products of 2×2 Hadamard blocks, so it is applied in O(d log d) time). W' is quantized with the same per-group symmetric affine RTN configuration as Arm 1. At inference, the dequantized Ŵ' is multiplied by H on the activation side: Ŷ = X H Ŵ'^T, exploiting H = H^T and H^T H = I. The Hadamard application to activations is a runtime arithmetic operation, not activation quantization, so this arm respects the weight-only constraint. Note that the full QuaRot system also includes SmoothQuant activation smoothing; that component is an activation-side technique and is explicitly out of scope here, so this arm is the paper's weight-only component (Hadamard + RTN). This scoping is flagged as assumption A12 and as limitation L1.

Arm 4, Hadamard-GPTQ: the same rotation W' = W H is applied first, and GPTQ is then run on the rotated model — critically, the per-layer Hessian is recomputed on the rotated network (a forward pass of the rotated model over the calibration set), so the Hessian reflects the rotated weight/activation geometry rather than being carried over from the unrotated model. This arm differs from Arm 2 by exactly the rotation, and is the clean ablation that isolates the Hadamard step at fixed algorithm. It is the central comparison for part (a).

### 2.3 Model selection and justification

Three models are used: LLaMA-2-7B, LLaMA-2-13B, and Mistral-7B-v0.1. The justification is threefold. First, the QuaRot paper reports results on LLaMA-2, LLaMA-3, and Mistral, so using the same families makes the design's claims source-consistent and permits direct comparison with published numbers. Second, 7–13B models are the scale at which weight-outlier structure is pronounced and 2-bit quantization is visibly destructive; smaller models show the phenomenon less sharply. Third, including two different architectures (LLaMA and Mistral, with different attention variants and vocabularies) tests whether the conclusion is family-specific, which is necessary before claiming that QuaRot "stabilizes" 2–4 bit quantization generally rather than for one family. A 3B model would have been the minimal-budget alternative and a 70B model the maximal-strength alternative; both are rejected on budget grounds (Section 6) and noted as assumption A2.

### 2.4 Calibration data (GPTQ arms only)

RTN and QuaRot require no calibration. GPTQ and Hadamard-GPTQ use a fixed calibration set: 256 sequences of 2048 tokens sampled from the C4 validation split (en-10.0.0), using the standard GPTQ sampling procedure with a fixed sampling seed (42) and standard tokenization per model. The same calibration set is used for every model, every bit-width, and every seed of the two GPTQ arms, so calibration is a controlled variable, not a free one. Hadamard-GPTQ uses the identical sampling seed and sequences; only the forward pass (hence the Hessian) differs because the weights are rotated.

### 2.5 Seed strategy

The two rotation arms depend on the random sign matrices S₁, S₂. For each (model, W) cell, K = 5 independent Hadamard seeds are drawn from a documented list (e.g., 0–4), and each seed produces a fully independent quantized model and evaluation. This matters most at 2 bits, where rotation variance is largest and "stabilization" claims would otherwise amount to a single lucky draw; K = 5 supports variance estimates and paired tests. RTN and GPTQ are deterministic under fixed configuration and calibration, so they require a single run per cell. ## 3. Controls

Every variable that is not the target of a comparison is held constant across arms, and each control is listed with the reason it must be controlled. Group size g = 128 is identical across all four arms, because group size independently changes quantization granularity and would otherwise confound the method effect; a g ∈ {64, 256} sensitivity sweep is listed as assumption A7 but is not in the main design. Symmetric per-group affine scaling is used by all arms, because mixing symmetric and asymmetric codebooks would introduce a second algorithmic difference. The layer set (all linears including lm_head, embeddings FP16) is identical, because different layer coverage changes total effective bit-count and quality. The FP16/BF16 reference is the original, unmodified checkpoint for each model, evaluated with identical batching, sequence length, and prompt templates as the quantized models, so that every degradation number is a within-model difference. The calibration set is fixed in content, size, order, and sampling seed for both GPTQ arms, because GPTQ quality is sensitive to calibration data and an uncontrolled difference would corrupt the GPTQ-vs-Hadamard-GPTQ contrast. Finally, the bit-width is applied identically to every arm, and dequantization at inference uses the same FP16 dequantized matmul in all arms, so the measured differences come from the quantization method alone, not from inference precision.

## 4. Evaluation protocol

### 4.1 Language-modeling perplexity

Zero-shot perplexity is computed on three held-out sets: WikiText-2 (test), C4 (validation, 256K-token window), and PTB (test), using the standard next-token evaluation with sequence length 2048 and batch 8, identical for FP16 and all quantized models. ### 4.2 Zero-shot task suite

Six zero-shot tasks are evaluated with the lm-evaluation-harness, greedy decoding, default templates: LAMBADA (last-word prediction), PIQA (physical commonsense), ARC-e (science reasoning), WinoGrande (coreference), TruthfulQA (multiple-choice), and RTE (entailment). Accuracy is reported per task as FP16 value and Δaccuracy. The suite mixes generation-style and multiple-choice formats and spans commonsense, reasoning, and truthfulness, so that "quality" is not a single-number construct.

### 4.3 FP16 reference

For each model, the unmodified checkpoint is evaluated once on all three perplexity sets and all six tasks, with the exact protocol of 4.1 and 4.2. These nine numbers per model are the denominator of every degradation metric and the anchor of the failure rule; they are computed once and reused, never re-sampled.

### 4.4 Mechanism diagnostics (for part (a))

Three weight-level measurements are taken per layer, per model, and per arm: (i) outlier statistics — the ratio of maximum to mean absolute weight magnitude, the kurtosis of the weight distribution, and the effective number of bits (the entropy of the quantization codebook usage, i.e., how many of the 2^W codes are actually used, or equivalently 1 − normalized quantization MSE) — computed both on the original weights and, for the rotation arms, on the rotated weights W H; (ii) per-layer relative quantization error ‖Q(W) − W‖_F / ‖W‖_F (and, for rotation arms, ‖Q(WH)H^T − W‖_F / ‖W‖_F, which is the error the model actually sees); (iii) the Spearman correlation, across layers, between each layer's pre-rotation outlier ratio and its pre-rotation quantization error, and the same correlation computed post-rotation for the rotation arms. The predicted signature of the mechanism is: pre-rotation, high outlier ratio correlates strongly with high quantization error; post-rotation, outlier ratios are compressed across layers, the correlation weakens, and per-layer error drops in absolute terms. If QuaRot beats RTN but this signature is absent, the gain has a different cause and part (a) must be answered accordingly — the diagnostics are what make the "how" question answerable rather than merely correlational.

## 5. Analysis plan

### 5(a) Attributing quality gains to the Hadamard rotation

The rotation effect is estimated from two contrasts at each (model, W): C1 = RTN − QuaRot, which isolates rotation under RTN, and C2 = GPTQ − Hadamard-GPTQ, which isolates rotation under GPTQ. The causal chain is checked in three steps. Step 1 (rotation → outliers): compare pre/post-rotation outlier statistics; the expected result is a large drop in max/mean ratio and kurtosis in the rotated weights. Step 2 (outliers → error): compare the layer-level error-vs-outlier correlation pre- vs. post-rotation and the absolute per-layer relative quantization error of QuaRot vs. RTN and Hadamard-GPTQ vs. GPTQ; the expected result is a weaker correlation and lower error after rotation. Step 3 (error → quality): compare ΔPPL and Δaccuracy of the paired contrasts C1 and C2; the expected result is that the arms with lower weight-level error have lower quality degradation. If C1 and C2 both favor the rotated arm and steps 1–2 show the diagnostic signature, the gain is attributed to the rotation specifically; if only C1 (or only C2) favors rotation, the effect is algorithm-conditional; if the diagnostics show no outlier compression, the claim of part (a) is not supported and the design has failed in the informative direction.

### 5(b) Operational failure definition and sensitivity analysis

A method is declared to **fail** at a (model, W, metric) cell if any of the following holds: ΔPPL > 100% over the FP16 reference, or absolute PPL > 10, or Δaccuracy > 20 percentage points on any of the six tasks. The three clauses are pre-registered together with their rationale: the relative PPL clause captures multiplicative collapse (the typical 2-bit GPTQ/RTN failure mode), the absolute PPL clause captures cases where the FP16 baseline is already weak, and the accuracy clause captures task-level collapse that perplexity may miss. Part (b) is then answered by tabulating, for each method and each W ∈ {4, 3, 2}, the fraction of cells across the 3 models × 9 metrics in which the method fails, plus the worst-cell degradation. QuaRot "stabilizes" 2–3 bit quantization if its failure fraction at W = 2 and W = 3 is materially lower than both RTN's and GPTQ's, and "improves" if its mean degradation at those widths is lower than both baselines'. A sensitivity analysis repeats the failure tabulation at 50% and 150% of each threshold (i.e., ΔPPL > 50%/150%, PPL > 5/15, Δacc > 10/30 pts) to show that the conclusion is not an artifact of the exact cutoff. The pre-registration of the thresholds and the sensitivity sweep are the guard against post-hoc threshold shopping.

### 5(c) Statistical tests, effect sizes, and confidence intervals

All method comparisons are paired within (model, W, seed) cells: the two arms in a contrast are evaluated on identical data with identical protocol, so per-cell paired differences are the unit of analysis. For each contrast and metric, the paired difference (e.g., ΔPPL_GPTQ − ΔPPL_HadGPTQ at W, model, seed) is tested with the Wilcoxon signed-rank test (non-parametric because 2-bit degradation distributions are heavy-tailed and n per contrast is small: 5 seeds × 3 models = 15 pairs for rotation arms, 3 pairs for the deterministic-arm contrasts — the latter are reported descriptively with CIs rather than tested), with the rank-biserial correlation r as the effect size. 95% confidence intervals are computed by non-parametric bootstrap (10,000 resamples over the seed × model pairs) on the mean paired difference. Because the full analysis involves many cells (4 methods × 3 W × 3 models × 9 metrics), no multiplicity correction is applied to the primary table, but a Bonferroni-corrected version of the W = 2 and W = 3 comparisons is reported as a robustness check, and all cells — including null ones — are reported in the main table.
